entries.title: The Ninja build system
entries.text: & 10; Introduction & 10; & 10; Ninja is yet another build system. It takes as input the& 10;interdependencies of files (typically source code and output& 10;executables) and orchestrates building them, quickly . & 10; Ninja joins a sea of other build systems. Its distinguishing goal is& 10;to be fast. It is born from& 10; my& 10;work on the Chromium browser project , which has over 30,000 source& 10;files and whose other build systems (including one built from custom& 10;non-recursive Makefiles) would take ten seconds to start building& 10;after changing one file. Ninja is under a second. & 10; & 10; Philosophical overview & 10; Where other build systems are high-level languages, Ninja aims to be& 10;an assembler. & 10; Build systems get slow when they need to make decisions. When you are& 10;in an edit-compile cycle you want it to be as fast as possible — you& 10;want the build system to do the minimum work necessary to figure out& 10;what needs to be built immediately. & 10; Ninja contains the barest functionality necessary to describe& 10;arbitrary dependency graphs. Its lack of syntax makes it impossible& 10;to express complex decisions. & 10; Instead, Ninja is intended to be used with a separate program& 10;generating its input files. The generator program (like the& 10; ./configure found in autotools projects) can analyze system& 10;dependencies and make as many decisions as possible up front so that& 10;incremental builds stay fast. Going beyond autotools, even build-time& 10;decisions like "which compiler flags should I use?" or "should I& 10;build a debug or release-mode binary?" belong in the .ninja file& 10;generator. & 10; & 10; & 10; Design goals & 10; Here are the design goals of Ninja: & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;very fast (i.e., instant) incremental builds, even for very large& 10; projects.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;very little policy about how code is built. Different projects and& 10; higher-level build systems have different opinions about how code& 10; should be built; for example, should built objects live alongside& 10; the sources or should all build output go into a separate directory?& 10; Is there a "package" rule that builds a distributable package of& 10; the project? Sidestep these decisions by trying to allow either to& 10; be implemented, rather than choosing, even if that results in& 10; more verbosity.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;get dependencies correct, and in particular situations that are& 10; difficult to get right with Makefiles (e.g. outputs need an implicit& 10; dependency on the command line used to generate them; to build C& 10; source code you need to use gcc’s -M flags for header& 10; dependencies).& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;when convenience and speed are in conflict, prefer speed.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Some explicit non-goals : & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;convenient syntax for writing build files by hand. You should& 10; generate your ninja files using another program . This is how we& 10; can sidestep many policy decisions.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;built-in rules. Out of the box, Ninja has no rules for& 10; e.g. compiling C code. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;build-time customization of the build. Options belong in& 10; the program that generates the ninja files .& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;build-time decision-making ability such as conditionals or search& 10; paths. Making decisions is slow. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; To restate, Ninja is faster than other build systems because it is& 10;painfully simple. You must tell Ninja exactly what to do when you& 10;create your project’s .ninja files. & 10; & 10; & 10; Comparison to Make & 10; Ninja is closest in spirit and functionality to Make, relying on& 10;simple dependencies between file timestamps. & 10; But fundamentally, make has a lot of features : suffix rules,& 10;functions, built-in rules that e.g. search for RCS files when building& 10;source. Make’s language was designed to be written by humans. Many& 10;projects find make alone adequate for their build problems. & 10; In contrast, Ninja has almost no features; just those necessary to get& 10;builds correct while punting most complexity to generation of the& 10;ninja input files. Ninja by itself is unlikely to be useful for most& 10;projects. & 10; Here are some of the features Ninja adds to Make. (These sorts of& 10;features can often be implemented using more complicated Makefiles,& 10;but they are not part of make itself.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Ninja has special support for discovering extra dependencies at build& 10; time, making it easy to get header dependencies & 10; correct for C/C++ code.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;A build edge may have multiple outputs.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Outputs implicitly depend on the command line that was used to generate& 10; them, which means that changing e.g. compilation flags will cause& 10; the outputs to rebuild.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Output directories are always implicitly created before running the& 10; command that relies on them.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Rules can provide shorter descriptions of the command being run, so& 10; you can print e.g. CC foo.o instead of a long command line while& 10; building.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Builds are always run in parallel, based by default on the number of& 10; CPUs your system has. Underspecified build dependencies will result& 10; in incorrect builds.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Command output is always buffered. This means commands running in& 10; parallel don’t interleave their output, and when a command fails we& 10; can print its failure output next to the full command line that& 10; produced the failure.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Using Ninja for your project & 10; & 10; Ninja currently works on Unix-like systems and Windows. It’s seen the& 10;most testing on Linux (and has the best performance there) but it runs& 10;fine on Mac OS X and FreeBSD. & 10; If your project is small, Ninja’s speed impact is likely unnoticeable.& 10;(However, even for small projects it sometimes turns out that Ninja’s& 10;limited syntax forces simpler build rules that result in faster& 10;builds.) Another way to say this is that if you’re happy with the& 10;edit-compile cycle time of your project already then Ninja won’t help. & 10; There are many other build systems that are more user-friendly or& 10;featureful than Ninja itself. For some recommendations: the Ninja& 10;author found the tup build system influential& 10;in Ninja’s design, and thinks redo 's& 10;design is quite clever. & 10; Ninja’s benefit comes from using it in conjunction with a smarter& 10;meta-build system. & 10; & 10; & 10; gn & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The meta-build system used to& 10;generate build files for Google Chrome and related projects (v8,& 10;node.js), as well as Google Fuchsia. gn can generate Ninja files for& 10;all platforms supported by Chrome.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; CMake & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;A widely used meta-build system that& 10;can generate Ninja files on Linux as of CMake version 2.8.8. Newer versions& 10;of CMake support generating Ninja files on Windows and Mac OS X too.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; others & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Ninja ought to fit perfectly into other meta-build software& 10;like premake . If you do this work,& 10;please let us know!& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Running Ninja & 10; Run ninja . By default, it looks for a file named build.ninja in& 10;the current directory and builds all out-of-date targets. You can& 10;specify which targets (files) to build as command line arguments. & 10; There is also a special syntax target^ for specifying a target& 10;as the first output of some rule containing the source you put in& 10;the command line, if one exists. For example, if you specify target as& 10; foo.c^ then foo.o will get built (assuming you have those targets& 10;in your build files). & 10; ninja -h prints help output. Many of Ninja’s flags intentionally& 10;match those of Make; e.g ninja -C build -j 20 changes into the& 10; build directory and runs 20 build commands in parallel. (Note that& 10;Ninja defaults to running commands in parallel anyway, so typically& 10;you don’t need to pass -j .) & 10; & 10; & 10; GNU Jobserver support & 10; Since version 1.13., Ninja builds can follow the& 10; GNU Make jobserver & 10;client protocol. This is useful when Ninja is invoked as part of a larger& 10;build system controlled by a top-level GNU Make instance, or any other& 10;jobserver pool implementation, as it allows better coordination between& 10;concurrent build tasks. & 10; This feature is automatically enabled under the following conditions: & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Dry-run (i.e. -n or --dry-run ) is not enabled.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;No explicit job count (e.g. -j<COUNT> ) is passed on the command& 10; line.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The MAKEFLAGS environment variable is defined and describes a valid& 10; jobserver mode using --jobserver-auth=SEMAPHORE_NAME on Windows, or& 10; --jobserver-auth=fifo:PATH on Posix.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; In this case, Ninja will use the jobserver pool of job slots to control& 10;parallelism, instead of its default parallel implementation. & 10; Note that load-average limitations (i.e. when using -l<count> )& 10;are still being enforced in this mode. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Important & 10; & 10; On Posix, only the FIFO-based version of the protocol, which is& 10;implemented by GNU Make 4.4 and higher, is supported. Ninja will detect& 10;when a pipe-based jobserver is being used (i.e. when MAKEFLAGS contains& 10; --jobserver-auth=<read>,<write> ) and will print a warning, but will& 10;otherwise ignore it. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Environment variables & 10; Ninja supports two environment variables to control its behavior:& 10; NINJA_STATUS , the progress status printed before the rule being run. & 10; Several placeholders are available: & 10; & 10; & 10; %s & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The number of started edges.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %t & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The total number of edges that must be run to complete the build.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %p & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The percentage of finished edges.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %r & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The number of currently running edges.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %u & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The number of remaining edges to start.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %f & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The number of finished edges.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %o & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Overall rate of finished edges per second& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %c & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Current rate of finished edges per second (average over builds& 10;specified by -j or its default)& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %e & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Elapsed time in seconds. (Available since Ninja 1.2.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %E & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Remaining time (ETA) in seconds. (Available since Ninja 1.12.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %w & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Elapsed time in [h:]mm:ss format. (Available since Ninja 1.12.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %W & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Remaining time (ETA) in [h:]mm:ss format. (Available since Ninja 1.12.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %P & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;The percentage (in ppp% format) of time elapsed out of predicted total runtime. (Available since Ninja 1.12.) & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; %% & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;A plain % character.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; The default progress status is "[%f/%t] " (note the trailing space& 10;to separate from the build rule). Another example of possible progress status& 10;could be "[%u/%r/%f] " . & 10; If MAKEFLAGS is defined in the environment, if may alter how& 10;Ninja dispatches parallel build commands. See the GNU Jobserver support& 10;section for details. & 10; & 10; & 10; Extra tools & 10; The -t flag on the Ninja command line runs some tools that we have& 10;found useful during Ninja’s development. The current tools are: & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; query & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;dump the inputs and outputs of a given target.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; browse & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;browse the dependency graph in a web browser. Clicking a& 10;file focuses the view on that file, showing inputs and outputs. This& 10;feature requires a Python installation. By default, port 8000 is used& 10;and a web browser will be opened. This can be changed as follows:& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja& 32;-t& 32;browse& 32;--port=8000& 32;--no-browser& 32;mytarget & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; graph & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;output a file in the syntax used by graphviz , an automatic& 10;graph layout tool. Use it like:& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja& 32;-t& 32;graph& 32;mytarget& 32; & 32;dot& 32;-Tpng& 32;-ograph.png & 10; & 10; In the Ninja source tree, ninja graph.png & 10;generates an image for Ninja itself. If no target is given generate a& 10;graph for all root targets. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; targets & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;output a list of targets either by rule or by depth. If used& 10;like ninja -t targets rule name it prints the list of targets& 10;using the given rule to be built. If no rule is given, it prints the source& 10;files (the leaves of the graph). If used like& 10; ninja -t targets depth digit it& 10;prints the list of targets in a depth-first manner starting by the root& 10;targets (the ones with no outputs). Indentation is used to mark dependencies.& 10;If the depth is zero it prints all targets. If no arguments are provided& 10; ninja -t targets depth 1 is assumed. In this mode targets may be listed& 10;several times. If used like this ninja -t targets all it& 10;prints all the targets available without indentation and it is faster& 10;than the depth mode.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; commands & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;given a list of targets, print a list of commands which, if& 10;executed in order, may be used to rebuild those targets, assuming that all& 10;output files are out of date.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; inputs & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;given a list of targets, print a list of all inputs used to& 10;rebuild those targets.& 10; Available since Ninja 1.11. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; multi-inputs & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;print one or more sets of inputs required to build targets.& 10;Each line will consist of a target, a delimiter, an input and a terminator character.& 10;The list produced by the tool can be helpful if one would like to know which targets& 10;that are affected by a certain input.& 10; & 10; The output will be a series of lines with the following elements: & 10; & 10; & 10; <target>& 32;<delimiter>& 32;<input>& 32;<terminator> & 10; & 10; The default <delimiter> is a single TAB character.& 10;The delimiter can be modified to any string using the --delimiter argument. & 10; The default <terminator> is a line terminator (i.e. \n on Posix and \r\n on Windows).& 10;The terminator can be changed to \0 by using the --print0 argument. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Example usage of the multi-inputs tool: & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja& 32;-t& 32;multi-inputs& 32;target1& 32;target2& 32;target3 & 10; & 10; Example of produced output from the multi-inputs tool: & 10; & 10; & 10; target1& 32;file1.c& 10;target2& 32;file1.c& 10;target2& 32;file2.c& 10;target3& 32;file1.c& 10;target3& 32;file2.c& 10;target3& 32;file3.c & 10; & 10; Note that a given input may appear for several targets if it is used by more& 10;than one targets. & 10; Available since Ninja 1.13. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; clean & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;remove built files. By default, it removes all built files& 10;except for those created by the generator. Adding the -g flag also& 10;removes built files created by the generator (see the rule reference for the generator attribute ). Additional arguments are& 10;targets, which removes the given targets and recursively all files& 10;built for them.& 10; & 10; If used like ninja -t clean -r rules it removes all files built using& 10;the given rules. & 10; Files created but not referenced in the graph are not removed. This& 10;tool takes in account the -v and the -n options (note that -n & 10;implies -v ). & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; cleandead & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;remove files produced by previous builds that are no longer in the& 10;build file. Available since Ninja 1.10. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; compdb & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;given a list of rules, each of which is expected to be a& 10;C family language compiler rule whose first input is the name of the& 10;source file, prints on standard output a compilation database in the& 10; JSON format expected& 10;by the Clang tooling interface.& 10; Available since Ninja 1.2. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; compdb-targets & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;like compdb , but takes a list of targets instead of rules,& 10;and expects at least one target. The resulting compilation database contains& 10;all commands required to build the indicated targets, and only those& 10;commands.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; deps & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;show all dependencies stored in the .ninja_deps file. When given a& 10;target, show just the target’s dependencies. Available since Ninja 1.4. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; missingdeps & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;given a list of targets, look for targets that depend on& 10;a generated file, but do not have a properly (possibly transitive) dependency& 10;on the generator. Such targets may cause build flakiness on clean builds.& 10; & 10; The broken targets can be found assuming deps log / depfile dependency& 10;information is correct. Any target that depends on a generated file (output& 10;of a generator-target) implicitly, but does not have an explicit or order-only& 10;dependency path to the generator-target, is considered broken. & 10; The tool’s findings can be verified by trying to build the listed targets in& 10;a clean outdir without building any other targets. The build should fail for& 10;each of them with a missing include error or equivalent pointing to the& 10;generated file.& 10; Available since Ninja 1.11. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; recompact & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;recompact the .ninja_deps file. Available since Ninja 1.4. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; restat & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;updates all recorded file modification timestamps in the .ninja_log & 10;file. Available since Ninja 1.10. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; rules & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;output the list of all rules. It can be used to know which rule name& 10;to pass to ninja -t targets rule name or ninja -t compdb . Adding the -d & 10;flag also prints the description of the rules.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; msvc & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Available on Windows hosts only.& 10;Helper tool to invoke the cl.exe compiler with a pre-defined set of& 10;environment variables, as in:& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja& 32;-t& 32;msvc& 32;-e& 32;ENVFILE& 32;--& 32;cl.exe& 32;<arguments> & 10; & 10; Where ENVFILE is a binary file that contains an environment block suitable& 10;for CreateProcessA() on Windows (i.e. a series of zero-terminated strings that& 10;look like NAME=VALUE, followed by an extra zero terminator). Note that this uses& 10;the local codepage encoding. & 10; This tool also supports a deprecated way of parsing the compiler’s output when& 10;the /showIncludes flag is used, and generating a GCC-compatible depfile from it: & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja& 32;-t& 32;msvc& 32;-o& 32;DEPFILE& 32;[-p& 32;STRING]& 32;--& 32;cl.exe& 32;/showIncludes& 32;<arguments> & 10; & 10; When using this option, -p STRING can be used to pass the localized line prefix& 10;that cl.exe uses to output dependency information. For English-speaking regions& 10;this is "Note: including file: " without the double quotes, but will be different& 10;for other regions. & 10; Note that Ninja supports this natively now, with the use of deps = msvc and& 10; msvc_deps_prefix in Ninja files. Native support also avoids launching an extra& 10;tool process each time the compiler must be called, which can speed up builds& 10;noticeably on Windows. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; wincodepage & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Available on Windows hosts ( since Ninja 1.11 ).& 10;Prints the Windows code page whose encoding is expected in the build file.& 10;The output has the form:& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Build& 32;file& 32;encoding:& 32;<codepage> & 10; & 10; Additional lines may be added in future versions of Ninja. & 10; The <codepage> is one of: & 10; & 10; & 10; UTF-8 & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Encode as UTF-8.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ANSI & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;Encode to the system-wide ANSI code page.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Writing your own Ninja files & 10; & 10; The remainder of this manual is only useful if you are constructing& 10;Ninja files yourself: for example, if you’re writing a meta-build& 10;system or supporting a new language. & 10; & 10; Conceptual overview & 10; Ninja evaluates a graph of dependencies between files, and runs& 10;whichever commands are necessary to make your build target up to date& 10;as determined by file modification times. If you are familiar with& 10;Make, Ninja is very similar. & 10; A build file (default name: build.ninja ) provides a list of rules — short names for longer commands, like how to run the compiler — along with a list of build statements saying how to build files& 10;using the rules — which rule to apply to which inputs to produce& 10;which outputs. & 10; Conceptually, build statements describe the dependency graph of your& 10;project, while rule statements describe how to generate the files& 10;along a given edge of the graph. & 10; & 10; & 10; Syntax example & 10; Here’s a basic .ninja file that demonstrates most of the syntax.& 10;It will be used as an example for the following sections. & 10; & 10; & 10; cflags& 32;=& 32;-Wall& 10;& 10;rule& 32;cc& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;gcc& 32;$cflags& 32;-c& 32;$in& 32;-o& 32;$out& 10;& 10;build& 32;foo.o:& 32;cc& 32;foo.c & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; Variables & 10; Despite the non-goal of being convenient to write by hand, to keep& 10;build files readable (debuggable), Ninja supports declaring shorter& 10;reusable names for strings. A declaration like the following & 10; & 10; & 10; cflags& 32;=& 32;-g & 10; & 10; can be used on the right side of an equals sign, dereferencing it with& 10;a dollar sign, like this: & 10; & 10; & 10; rule& 32;cc& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;gcc& 32;$cflags& 32;-c& 32;$in& 32;-o& 32;$out & 10; & 10; Variables can also be referenced using curly braces like ${in} . & 10; Variables might better be called "bindings", in that a given variable& 10;cannot be changed, only shadowed. There is more on how shadowing works& 10;later in this document. & 10; & 10; & 10; Rules & 10; Rules declare a short name for a command line. They begin with a line& 10;consisting of the rule keyword and a name for the rule. Then& 10;follows an indented set of variable = value lines. & 10; The basic example above declares a new rule named cc , along with the& 10;command to run. In the context of a rule, the command variable& 10;defines the command to run, $in expands to the list of& 10;input files ( foo.c ), and $out to the output files ( foo.o ) for the& 10;command. A full list of special variables is provided in& 10; the reference . & 10; & 10; & 10; Build statements & 10; Build statements declare a relationship between input and output& 10;files. They begin with the build keyword, and have the format& 10; build outputs : rulename inputs . Such a declaration says that& 10;all of the output files are derived from the input files. When the& 10;output files are missing or when the inputs change, Ninja will run the& 10;rule to regenerate the outputs. & 10; The basic example above describes how to build foo.o , using the cc & 10;rule. & 10; In the scope of a build block (including in the evaluation of its& 10;associated rule ), the variable $in is the list of inputs and the& 10;variable $out is the list of outputs. & 10; A build statement may be followed by an indented set of key = value & 10;pairs, much like a rule. These variables will shadow any variables& 10;when evaluating the variables in the command. For example: & 10; & 10; & 10; cflags& 32;=& 32;-Wall& 32;-Werror& 10;rule& 32;cc& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;gcc& 32;$cflags& 32;-c& 32;$in& 32;-o& 32;$out& 10;& 10; & 32;If& 32;left& 32;unspecified,& 32;builds& 32;get& 32;the& 32;outer& 32;$cflags.& 10;build& 32;foo.o:& 32;cc& 32;foo.c& 10;& 10; & 32;But& 32;you& 32;can& 32;shadow& 32;variables& 32;like& 32;cflags& 32;for& 32;a& 32;particular& 32;build.& 10;build& 32;special.o:& 32;cc& 32;special.c& 10;& 32;& 32;cflags& 32;=& 32;-Wall& 10;& 10; & 32;The& 32;variable& 32;was& 32;only& 32;shadowed& 32;for& 32;the& 32;scope& 32;of& 32;special.o;& 10; & 32;Subsequent& 32;build& 32;lines& 32;get& 32;the& 32;outer& 32;(original)& 32;cflags.& 10;build& 32;bar.o:& 32;cc& 32;bar.c & 10; & 10; For more discussion of how scoping works, consult the reference . & 10; If you need more complicated information passed from the build& 10;statement to the rule (for example, if the rule needs "the file& 10;extension of the first input"), pass that through as an extra& 10;variable, like how cflags is passed above. & 10; If the top-level Ninja file is specified as an output of any build& 10;statement and it is out of date, Ninja will rebuild and reload it& 10;before building the targets requested by the user. & 10; & 10; & 10; Generating Ninja files from code & 10; misc/ninja_syntax.py in the Ninja distribution is a tiny Python& 10;module to facilitate generating Ninja files. It allows you to make& 10;Python calls like ninja.rule(name='foo', command='bar',& 10;depfile='$out.d') and it will generate the appropriate syntax. Feel& 10;free to just inline it into your project’s build system if it’s& 10;useful. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; More details & 10; & 10; & 10; The phony rule & 10; The special rule name phony can be used to create aliases for other& 10;targets. For example: & 10; & 10; & 10; build& 32;foo:& 32;phony& 32;some/file/in/a/faraway/subdir/foo & 10; & 10; This makes ninja foo build the longer path. Semantically, the& 10; phony rule is equivalent to a plain rule where the command does& 10;nothing, but phony rules are handled specially in that they aren’t& 10;printed when run, logged (see below), nor do they contribute to the& 10;command count printed as part of the build process. & 10; When a phony target is used as an input to another build rule, the& 10;other build rule will, semantically, consider the inputs of the& 10; phony rule as its own. Therefore, phony rules can be used to group& 10;inputs, e.g. header files. & 10; phony can also be used to create dummy targets for files which& 10;may not exist at build time. If a phony build statement is written& 10;without any dependencies, the target will be considered out of date if& 10;it does not exist. This may include additional& 10;implicit inputs and/or outputs. Ninja will update the build graph& 10;accordingly and the build will proceed as if the information was known& 10;originally. & 10; & 10; Dyndep file reference & 10; Files specified by dyndep bindings use the same lexical syntax & 10;as ninja build files and have the following layout. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;A version number in the form <major>[.<minor>][<suffix>] :& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja_dyndep_version& 32;=& 32;1 & 10; & 10; Currently the version number must always be 1 or 1.0 but may have& 10;an arbitrary suffix. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;One or more build statements of the form:& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; build& 32;out& 32; & 32;imp-outs...& 32;:& 32;dyndep& 32; & 32;imp-ins... & 10; & 10; Every statement must specify exactly one explicit output and must use& 10;the rule name dyndep . The imp-outs... and imp-ins... portions& 10;are optional. & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;An optional restat variable binding on each build statement.& 10; & 10; & 10; & 10; The build statements in a dyndep file must have a one-to-one correspondence& 10;to build statements in the ninja build file that name the& 10;dyndep file in a dyndep binding. No dyndep build statement may be omitted& 10;and no extra build statements may be specified. & 10; & 10; & 10; Dyndep Examples & 10; & 10; Fortran Modules & 10; Consider a Fortran source file foo.f90 that provides a module& 10; foo.mod (an implicit output of compilation) and another source file& 10; bar.f90 that uses the module (an implicit input of compilation). This& 10;implicit dependency must be discovered before we compile either source& 10;in order to ensure that bar.f90 never compiles before foo.f90 , and& 10;that bar.f90 recompiles when foo.mod changes. We can achieve this& 10;as follows: & 10; & 10; & 10; rule& 32;f95& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;f95& 32;-o& 32;$out& 32;-c& 32;$in& 10;rule& 32;fscan& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;fscan& 32;-o& 32;$out& 32;$in& 10;& 10;build& 32;foobar.dd:& 32;fscan& 32;foo.f90& 32;bar.f90& 10;& 10;build& 32;foo.o:& 32;f95& 32;foo.f90& 32; & 32;foobar.dd& 10;& 32;& 32;dyndep& 32;=& 32;foobar.dd& 10;build& 32;bar.o:& 32;f95& 32;bar.f90& 32; & 32;foobar.dd& 10;& 32;& 32;dyndep& 32;=& 32;foobar.dd & 10; & 10; In this example the order-only dependencies ensure that foobar.dd is& 10;generated before either source compiles. The hypothetical fscan tool& 10;scans the source files, assumes each will be compiled to a .o of the& 10;same name, and writes foobar.dd with content such as: & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja_dyndep_version& 32;=& 32;1& 10;build& 32;foo.o& 32; & 32;foo.mod:& 32;dyndep& 10;build& 32;bar.o:& 32;dyndep& 32; & 32;& 32;foo.mod & 10; & 10; Ninja will load this file to add foo.mod as an implicit output of& 10; foo.o and implicit input of bar.o . This ensures that the Fortran& 10;sources are always compiled in the proper order and recompiled when& 10;needed. & 10; & 10; & 10; Tarball Extraction & 10; Consider a tarball foo.tar that we want to extract. The extraction time& 10;can be recorded with a foo.tar.stamp file so that extraction repeats if& 10;the tarball changes, but we also would like to re-extract if any of the& 10;outputs is missing. However, the list of outputs depends on the content& 10;of the tarball and cannot be spelled out explicitly in the ninja build file.& 10;We can achieve this as follows: & 10; & 10; & 10; rule& 32;untar& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;tar& 32;xf& 32;$in& 32;&&& 32;touch& 32;$out& 10;rule& 32;scantar& 10;& 32;& 32;command& 32;=& 32;scantar& 32;--stamp=$stamp& 32;--dd=$out& 32;$in& 10;build& 32;foo.tar.dd:& 32;scantar& 32;foo.tar& 10;& 32;& 32;stamp& 32;=& 32;foo.tar.stamp& 10;build& 32;foo.tar.stamp:& 32;untar& 32;foo.tar& 32; & 32;foo.tar.dd& 10;& 32;& 32;dyndep& 32;=& 32;foo.tar.dd & 10; & 10; In this example the order-only dependency ensures that foo.tar.dd is& 10;built before the tarball extracts. The hypothetical scantar tool& 10;will read the tarball (e.g. via tar tf ) and write foo.tar.dd with& 10;content such as: & 10; & 10; & 10; ninja_dyndep_version& 32;=& 32;1& 10;build& 32;foo.tar.stamp& 32; & 32;file1.txt& 32;file2.txt& 32;:& 32;dyndep& 10;& 32;& 32;restat& 32;=& 32;1 & 10; & 10; Ninja will load this file to add file1.txt and file2.txt as implicit& 10;outputs of foo.tar.stamp , and to mark the build statement for restat .& 10;On future builds, if any implicit output is missing the tarball will be& 10;extracted again. The restat binding tells Ninja to tolerate the fact& 10;that the implicit outputs may not have modification times newer than& 10;the tarball itself (avoiding re-extraction on every build). & 10; & 10; & 10; & 10;
